stem: Which piece of apparatus is used to measure the volume of gas given off during a reaction?

options.content: a gas syringe
options.rationale: Its plunger moves out as gas collects, and the volume is read from the scale.

options.content: a thermometer
options.rationale: A thermometer measures temperature.

options.content: a top-pan balance
options.rationale: A balance measures mass, for the loss-in-mass method.

options.content: a pipette
options.rationale: A pipette measures a fixed volume of liquid.

explanation: A gas syringe (or an upturned measuring cylinder full of water) collects the gas so that its volume can be read at regular time intervals.

stem: Which is a suitable unit for the rate at which a gas is produced?

options.content: cm³
options.rationale: This is a unit of volume only.

options.content: cm³/s
options.rationale: Volume of gas divided by time.

options.content: s
options.rationale: This is a unit of time only.

options.content: g/cm³
options.rationale: This is a unit of density.

explanation: Rate = amount ÷ time, so for a gas the unit is volume per unit time, such as cm³/s or cm³/min.

stem: True or false: on a graph of volume of gas against time, the curve is steepest at the start of the reaction.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: the reactants are most concentrated at the start, so the rate is fastest then.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. The rate is fastest at the start, when the concentration of reactants is highest, so the curve is steepest there.

explanation: As the reactants are used up their concentration falls, collisions become less frequent and the curve gets less steep, until it is horizontal when the reaction stops.

stem: A reaction gives off 45 cm³ of gas in the first 30 seconds. Calculate the average rate of reaction over this time.
explanation: Average rate = volume ÷ time = 45 ÷ 30 = 1.5 cm³/s.

stem: Magnesium reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Why does the reaction slow down as time goes on?

options.content: Reactants are used up, so collisions become less frequent.
options.rationale: Fewer reacting particles per unit volume means fewer collisions per second.

options.content: The catalyst is gradually used up.
options.rationale: There is no catalyst in this reaction.

options.content: The temperature of the mixture rises.
options.rationale: A temperature rise would speed the reaction up, not slow it down.

options.content: The hydrogen produced reacts with the remaining magnesium.
options.rationale: Hydrogen does not react with magnesium.

explanation: As the reaction proceeds, the acid becomes less concentrated and the magnesium gets smaller. There are fewer collisions per second, so the rate falls until the magnesium (the limiting reactant) is used up.

stem: In the loss-in-mass method, why is a loose plug of cotton wool put in the neck of the flask?

options.content: It stops the gas from escaping, so the mass stays constant.
options.rationale: The gas must escape: its loss is what is measured.

options.content: It lets the gas escape but stops acid spray from leaving the flask.
options.rationale: Lost spray would make the mass loss too large.

options.content: It absorbs the gas so that it can be weighed.
options.rationale: Cotton wool does not absorb carbon dioxide.

options.content: It acts as a catalyst.
options.rationale: Cotton wool is not a catalyst.

explanation: The mass falls because carbon dioxide escapes. The cotton wool lets the gas out but traps droplets of acid that would otherwise spray out and add to the measured loss.

stem: Why is the loss-in-mass method **not** suitable for following the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid?

options.content: Hydrogen does not escape from the open flask at all.
options.rationale: Hydrogen escapes easily; it is just very light.

options.content: Magnesium gains mass as it reacts, because it absorbs the dilute acid.
options.rationale: Magnesium is used up; it does not gain mass.

options.content: Hydrogen is so light that the loss in mass is too small to measure.
options.rationale: A school balance cannot measure such tiny changes precisely.

options.content: The reaction is far too slow to measure this way.
options.rationale: The reaction is reasonably fast; the problem is the tiny mass of hydrogen.

explanation:
Hydrogen (Mr = 2) is so light that the total mass lost in a school experiment may be only a few hundredths of a gram. A gas syringe gives far more precise results for this reaction.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Compare the mass of a mole of hydrogen with a mole of carbon dioxide.

stem: In a disappearing-cross experiment with sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, the cross disappears after 50 s. Calculate the relative rate of reaction, using rate = 1/time.
explanation: Rate = 1 ÷ time = 1 ÷ 50 = 0.020 s⁻¹. A shorter time would give a larger value, showing a faster reaction.

stem: An experiment uses a strip of magnesium ribbon with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. It is repeated with a strip of the same ribbon that is **half as long**, and everything else the same. How does the second curve of volume of hydrogen against time compare with the first?

options.content: It is less steep at the start and levels off at half the volume.
options.rationale: Half the magnesium gives half the hydrogen, and its smaller surface area gives a slower rate.

options.content: It is steeper at the start and levels off at the same volume.
options.rationale: Less magnesium cannot give the same amount of hydrogen.

options.content: It is less steep at the start and levels off at the same volume.
options.rationale: Magnesium is the limiting reactant, so halving it halves the hydrogen.

options.content: It is the same as the first curve.
options.rationale: The amount of the limiting reactant has changed.

explanation: Magnesium is the limiting reactant, so half the magnesium gives half the final volume. A shorter strip also has a smaller surface area in contact with the acid, so the initial rate is lower.

stem: Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. The experiment is repeated with the same mass of the same chips but with **more concentrated** acid; the marble is the limiting reactant both times. How does the new curve of mass lost against time compare?

options.content: It is steeper at the start and levels off at a higher mass lost.
options.rationale: The marble is limiting, so the same amount of carbon dioxide forms.

options.content: It is less steep at the start and levels off at the same mass lost.
options.rationale: A higher concentration makes the reaction faster.

options.content: It is steeper at the start and levels off at the same mass lost.
options.rationale: More concentrated acid speeds the reaction, but the amount of marble is unchanged.

options.content: It is the same as the first curve.
options.rationale: A higher concentration changes the rate.

explanation: The final mass lost depends on the amount of marble, which has not changed. The more concentrated acid has more particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent and the curve is steeper at the start.
hints: Does a change of concentration change the amount of the limiting reactant?

stem:
Chipo adds calcium carbonate to excess dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe.

| Time / s | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 | 100 | 120 | 140 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Volume of carbon dioxide / cm³ | 0 | 30 | 52 | 68 | 78 | 84 | 86 | 86 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the total volume of carbon dioxide produced?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the average rate of reaction during the first 40 s.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the average rate of reaction between 40 s and 80 s.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the rate between 40 s and 80 s is lower than in the first 40 s.

points.description: The calcium carbonate / reactants are being used up (lower concentration of acid, less solid)
So there are fewer collisions per second (less frequent collisions)

parts.explanation: The reactants are being used up: there is less calcium carbonate and the acid is less concentrated. Particles collide less frequently, so the rate falls.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: At about what time did the reaction finish?

options.rationale: The volume is still increasing after 80 s.
The volume stops changing at 120 s.
The volume had already stopped changing at 120 s.
The volume increases from 84 to 86 cm³ after 100 s.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount, in moles, of carbon dioxide produced. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (One mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.)

explanation: The volume levels off at 86 cm³ at 120 s. First 40 s: 52 ÷ 40 = 1.3 cm³/s. From 40 s to 80 s: (78 − 52) ÷ 40 = 26 ÷ 40 = 0.65 cm³/s. The rate falls because the reactants are used up and collisions become less frequent. Moles of CO₂ = 86 ÷ 24 000 = 0.00358 mol.
hints: Average rate = change in volume ÷ change in time.
Read the final volume where the numbers stop changing.

stem:
Nyasha adds marble chips (calcium carbonate) to excess dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask on a balance, with cotton wool in the neck.

| Time / min | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mass of flask and contents / g | 152.40 | 151.88 | 151.52 | 151.28 | 151.14 | 151.10 | 151.10 |

options.content: The marble chips dissolve.
options.rationale: Dissolving does not change the total mass; something must leave the flask.

options.content: Water evaporates from the warm acid solution.
options.rationale: Evaporation is negligible compared with the gas lost.

options.content: Carbon dioxide gas escapes from the flask.
options.rationale: The gas leaves through the cotton wool.

options.content: The acid is neutralised.
options.rationale: Neutralisation alone does not remove mass from the flask.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total mass of carbon dioxide given off.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the average rate of reaction in the first 2 minutes, in g/min.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate that reacted. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: CO₂ = 44, CaCO₃ = 100)

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest one reason why the results might give a mass of carbon dioxide that is too low.

points.description: Some CO₂ escapes before the first reading / some CO₂ dissolves in the solution / gas lost before the cotton wool was added

parts.explanation: Some carbon dioxide escaped in the moment before the first reading was taken, and a little carbon dioxide stays dissolved in the solution.

explanation: The mass falls because carbon dioxide escapes. Total CO₂ = 152.40 − 151.10 = 1.30 g. First 2 minutes: (152.40 − 151.52) ÷ 2 = 0.88 ÷ 2 = 0.44 g/min. From CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, 1 mol CaCO₃ gives 1 mol CO₂: 1.30 ÷ 44 = 0.0295 mol, so mass of CaCO₃ = 0.0295 × 100 = 2.95 g.
hints: Mass lost = mass at the start − final mass.
1 mol of CaCO₃ produces 1 mol of CO₂.

stem:
A student plots a graph of the volume of hydrogen given off against time for magnesium reacting with dilute sulfuric acid. She draws two tangents to the curve.

- The tangent at **t = 0** passes through (0 s, 0 cm³) and (10 s, 40 cm³).
- The tangent at **t = 30 s** passes through (10 s, 22 cm³) and (50 s, 62 cm³).

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the initial rate of reaction from the tangent at t = 0.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the rate of reaction at t = 30 s.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the rate at 30 s is lower than the initial rate.

points.description: The acid/magnesium has been partly used up, so the concentration of acid is lower
Fewer particles per unit volume, so less frequent (successful) collisions

parts.explanation: By 30 s some of the reactants have been used up. The acid is less concentrated, so there are fewer acid particles per unit volume and collisions with the magnesium are less frequent.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The student collected the hydrogen in an upturned measuring cylinder full of water instead of a gas syringe. Which statement about this change is correct?

options.content: Much of the hydrogen dissolves in the water, so the volume is far too low.
options.rationale: Hydrogen is only very slightly soluble in water; this matters more for gases such as carbon dioxide.

options.content: The hydrogen reacts with the water in the cylinder.
options.rationale: Hydrogen does not react with water.

options.content: The method becomes more accurate because the water absorbs heat from the reaction.
options.rationale: Collecting over water does not make the results more accurate.

options.content: It still works (hydrogen barely dissolves), but readings are less precise.
options.rationale: Collecting over water is acceptable for hydrogen; a gas syringe is easier to read precisely.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest how the student could avoid losing gas at the very start of the experiment.

points.description: Put the acid and magnesium in separate parts (e.g. magnesium in a small tube) and mix them only after the bung is in place / tip the flask after sealing

parts.explanation: Place the magnesium in a small tube inside the flask, fit the bung, and then tip the flask to mix the reactants, so no gas escapes before the apparatus is sealed.

explanation:
The gradient of a tangent is the rate at that moment. At t = 0: (40 − 0) ÷ (10 − 0) = 4.0 cm³/s. At t = 30 s: (62 − 22) ÷ (50 − 10) = 40 ÷ 40 = 1.0 cm³/s. The rate falls because the reactants are being used up.

*Syllabus note: rates from tangents are for Cambridge IGCSE Extended candidates; the evaluation in (d) and (e) is Supplement content.*
hints: Gradient = change in volume ÷ change in time, using two points on the tangent.

stem: A student wants to measure the volume of **carbon dioxide** produced each minute as accurately as possible. Which method is best?

options.content: collecting the gas in a gas syringe
options.rationale: Gas syringes are precise and no carbon dioxide dissolves in water.

options.content: collecting the gas over water in an upturned measuring cylinder
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is slightly soluble in water, so some is lost.

options.content: counting the bubbles given off
options.rationale: Bubbles vary in size, so counting them is not a reliable measure of volume.

options.content: timing how long the solid takes to disappear
options.rationale: This gives only one overall time, not the volume each minute.

explanation:
A gas syringe measures the volume directly and precisely. Collecting carbon dioxide over water gives slightly low readings because some of the gas dissolves.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Which gas collection method avoids contact with water?

stem: In the disappearing-cross experiment, different students often record different times for the same mixture. What is the main reason?

options.content: The precipitate of sulfur forms at different rates for different observers.
options.rationale: The reaction rate does not depend on who is watching.

options.content: Deciding exactly when the cross can no longer be seen is a matter of judgement.
options.rationale: Eyesight, lighting and the angle of view all affect the result.

options.content: The stopwatch measures time inaccurately.
options.rationale: Stopwatches are far more precise than the judgement of the end point.

options.content: The sulfur dioxide produced hides the cross.
options.rationale: Sulfur dioxide is a colourless gas; the cloudiness is from the sulfur.

explanation:
The end point is subjective. Using the same observer, the same printed cross and the same lighting, or a light sensor instead of the eye, makes the results more reliable.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: What is the student actually judging?

stem: Complete the sentences about measuring rates by choosing the correct apparatus.

payload.template: The volume of gas produced can be measured with a {{blank:a}}. The loss in mass is measured with a {{blank:b}}. The time taken for a cross to disappear is measured with a {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Gas volume: gas syringe. Loss in mass: top-pan balance. Disappearing cross: stopwatch. In every method, time is measured with a stopwatch.

stem: Match each reaction to the most suitable way of following its rate.

left.content: magnesium + dilute hydrochloric acid (gives hydrogen, a very light gas)
sodium thiosulfate + dilute hydrochloric acid (gives a precipitate of sulfur)
marble chips + dilute hydrochloric acid in an open flask with cotton wool

right.content: collect the gas in a gas syringe
time how long it takes for a cross to be hidden
measure the loss in mass on a balance
measure the change in the length of the flask

explanation: Hydrogen is too light for the mass-loss method, so its volume is measured. The sulfur precipitate makes the mixture cloudy, so the disappearing cross is used. Carbon dioxide is heavy enough for the loss in mass to be measured on a balance.
hints: Think about what each reaction produces.

stem: Plan an experiment to find out how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of its reaction with magnesium ribbon. Use a gas syringe. Include the apparatus, what you would measure, how you would make it a fair test and how you would use your results. [6]

points.description: Apparatus: conical flask with bung and delivery tube connected to a gas syringe; stopwatch
Use the same length/mass of magnesium ribbon each time (acid in excess)
Use the same volume of acid, changing only its concentration (e.g. 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 mol/dm³)
Keep the temperature the same (e.g. room temperature)
Start the stopwatch when the magnesium is added and record the gas volume at regular intervals (e.g. every 10 s) until it stops changing
Plot volume against time for each concentration and compare the initial gradients / average rates (or time to collect a set volume)
Safety: eye protection; no flames near the hydrogen

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Set up a conical flask closed with a bung and delivery tube leading to a gas syringe. Put 50 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid in the flask, add a 3 cm strip of magnesium ribbon, quickly replace the bung and start the stopwatch. Record the volume of hydrogen every 10 seconds until it stops changing. Repeat with acid of concentrations 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mol/dm³. To keep the test fair, use the same length of magnesium ribbon from the same roll, the same volume of acid (in excess) and the same temperature each time. Plot a graph of volume against time for each concentration and compare the initial gradients, or calculate the average rate over the first 30 s, to see how the rate changes with concentration. Wear eye protection and keep flames away from the hydrogen.

explanation: A good plan changes only one variable (the acid concentration), measures the gas volume at regular time intervals, controls the other variables and explains how the rate will be compared.
hints: Name the independent, dependent and control variables.

stem: In a mass-loss experiment, 0.84 g of carbon dioxide is given off in the first 2.0 minutes. Calculate the average rate of reaction in **grams per second**.
explanation: 2.0 minutes = 120 s. Average rate = 0.84 ÷ 120 = 0.0070 g/s (which is 0.42 g/min).

stem: Experiment X is done at 25 °C. Experiment Y uses exactly the same amounts of the same reactants but at 45 °C. Which describes the curve for Y on a graph of volume of gas against time?

options.content: steeper at the start, levelling off at a larger final volume
options.rationale: Temperature does not change the amount of product.

options.content: less steep at the start, levelling off later at the same final volume
options.rationale: A higher temperature gives a faster rate, not a slower one.

options.content: the same as the curve for X
options.rationale: A 20 °C rise in temperature greatly increases the rate.

options.content: steeper at the start, levelling off sooner at the same final volume
options.rationale: Faster rate, same amount of limiting reactant.

explanation: At the higher temperature the reaction is faster, so the curve rises more steeply and the reaction finishes sooner. The amounts of reactants are the same, so the same final volume of gas is produced.
hints: Temperature affects the rate, not the amount of product.

stem: On a graph of the volume of gas given off against time, the curve eventually becomes horizontal. What does this show?

options.content: The reaction is going at its fastest rate.
options.rationale: A horizontal line means no more gas is being produced: the rate is zero.

options.content: Every reactant, including the one in excess, has been completely used up.
options.rationale: Only the limiting reactant runs out; some of the reactant in excess is left over.

options.content: The catalyst has been used up.
options.rationale: A catalyst is not used up, and many reactions have no catalyst.

options.content: The reaction has stopped because the limiting reactant has been used up.
options.rationale: No more gas forms, so the volume stays constant.

explanation: When the limiting reactant has all reacted, no more gas is produced, so the volume stays the same and the curve is horizontal. The reactant in excess is still present.
hints: What is happening to the volume of gas while the line is flat?
